meta.subtitle: Two quarters of GAAP profit and strong cash generation, set against revenue that lags volume and a concentrated customer base

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Marqeta HOLD with a $15 to $21 target range built around a Base case of $18. The 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 shows a business that is growing and has been profitable on a GAAP basis through the six months ended June 30, 2026: Q2'26 revenue of $176M rose 17% year on year and the quarter's operating margin was 2.1%. Three things keep us from buying. Processing volume is growing faster than revenue, which we think partly reflects how Revenue Share is priced. A small number of customers, Block among them, carry significant revenue, so any renegotiation can reset the model. And the market-cap figures behind the valuation rest on a vendor share count that the proxy does not confirm, a point the Valuation section sets out. Against that, the business converts revenue to free cash at a high rate and carries no reported debt, which limits how far a reasonable bear case can go. We would turn more constructive on a full GAAP-profitable year with revenue growth holding near the Q2'26 pace.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Marqeta, Inc. runs a cloud-based open API platform for card issuing and transaction processing, headquartered in Oakland, California and incorporated in 2010. Per the 10-Q MD&A, every customer takes issuer processor services as the core offering; customers can add Bank and Network Management, Program Management (chargebacks, dispute resolution, reconciliation, card fulfillment) and Value Added Services such as tokenization and real-time decisioning and fraud management. Net revenue has two components, platform services revenue, net, which carries Interchange Fees net of Revenue Share plus processing and other fees, and other services revenue, mainly card fulfillment; the MD&A excerpt does not size them. The company reports a single reportable segment. Verticals named in the company description include financial services, on-demand services, lending, expense management, e-commerce enablement and buy now, pay later providers.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Marqeta has posted GAAP profit in both quarters of 2026 while growing revenue in the high teens, and it converts revenue to free cash at a high rate. The shares trade near the low end of the 52-week range, yet the Street is mostly at Hold. Upside to the Street consensus target of $20.50 needs revenue growth to hold near the Q2'26 pace while operating costs stay contained. The widening gap between processing volume and revenue is the main risk to that path, and customer concentration is the second. We think risk and reward are roughly balanced at $16.55.

catalysts: A full GAAP-profitable year, visible as the TTM operating margin of -1.9% turning positive; the Financials section sets out the six-month results.
Revenue growth that holds near the Q2'26 pace of 17% rather than slowing to the +13% FY26E consensus; the Growth section covers the gap between volume and revenue.
Disclosure in a future filing of Block terms that do not cut pricing; the pack gives no renewal date, and the Risks section explains why it matters.
Repurchases paced to free cash flow rather than drawing on cash, discussed under Capital allocation.
risks: Customer concentration, with Block named among a few significant customers; see Risks.
Revenue growth lagging volume as customer pricing steps up with scale; see Growth.
A thinner liquidity buffer than in prior years; see the Balance sheet commentary.
Dual class voting that leaves outside holders little leverage; see Governance.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: The income statement turned positive in 2026, not just in one quarter. The 10-Q MD&A reports net income of $15,401 thousand for the six months ended June 30, 2026, after a loss of $8,907 thousand in the same period of 2025, and Q2'26 alone contributed $7,567 thousand. Q2'26 net revenue rose to $175,995 thousand from $150,392 thousand. Gross margin held at 69% in both Q2 periods, so the improvement came from below gross profit: total operating expenses rose to $118,237 thousand from $113,289 thousand, much slower than revenue. Adjusted EBITDA margin, a non-GAAP measure, moved to 21% from 19%. The trailing picture still lags, with a TTM operating margin of -1.9% and a net loss for FY25 as a whole, so two profitable quarters do not yet make a profitable year. The annual series also needs care. The 10-K risk factors attribute the FY24 revenue decrease primarily to the August 2023 Block Amendment, which both allowed reduced pricing and moved Cash App fees owed to Issuing Banks and Card Networks out of costs of revenue and into a reduction of net revenue from July 1, 2023. We read the gross margin step from 48.7% in FY23 to 69.4% in FY24 as largely a result of those moved costs, though the 10-K does not say so. Our view: the earnings trend is genuinely improving, but it rests on operating expense discipline that has to persist.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet carries no reported debt, and cash and short-term investments stood at $0.7B at FY25. The trend is the concern. Cash and short-term investments have fallen from $1.2B in FY21 and FY22, total equity has fallen from $1.6B in FY21 to $0.8B in FY25, and the current ratio dropped to 1.65 in FY25 from 3.37 a year earlier. The facts do not break out current liabilities, so we cannot say how much of the ratio's decline reflects settlement balances rather than lost cushion. The capital allocation discussion under Management explains where the cash went. The balance sheet remains sound, but it is no longer the excess-capital story it was in FY21.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Free cash flow is the strongest part of the case. FY25 free cash flow was $160.8M, an FCF margin of 25.7%, up from 11.0% in FY24, and capital expenditure is small. Operating cash flow and free cash flow are nearly identical across the five years, which fits an asset-light processor. The FCF margin runs well ahead of the GAAP operating margin, and the facts include no bridge between them, so we treat part of the FY25 cash strength as possible working-capital timing until a second year confirms it. Our view is that cash generation is real, but the FY25 margin is not a safe base to extrapolate. How that cash was spent is judged under Capital allocation.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On earnings the stock looks expensive and on cash it looks cheap, and the gap between the two is the valuation debate. Trailing P/E is 183.9x and EV/EBITDA is 62.9x because GAAP earnings are barely positive on a trailing basis. Forward P/E falls to 61.3x on the NTM view and ~33.1x on FY27E consensus EPS of $0.50, with FY26E EPS at $0.27; the vendor does not state whether these consensus figures are GAAP or adjusted, so we do not treat the forward multiples as GAAP-based. P/S is 2.5x and the TTM FCF yield is 11.5%. One caveat applies to all of these and to any comparison of cash with market value: the Quote derives ~104.1M shares from the ~$1.7B market cap, while the proxy reports 392,067,528 Class A and 32,808,210 Class B shares outstanding as of April 15, 2026. The sources do not explain the difference. We use the vendor market cap and multiples as given, but if the proxy count were the right basis, the FCF yield would be lower and P/S higher than shown. The Street is cautious, with 14 analysts at 3 Buy, 10 Hold and 1 Sell and a median target of $19.50.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Revenue growth holds near the Q2'26 pace and operating costs stay contained, so GAAP profit compounds toward FY27E consensus EPS of $0.50. Both conditions have to hold together. The shares rerate above the Street consensus target of $20.50 and above our $21 target high, within the Street's $17.00 to $28.00 range of analyst targets.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue lands near FY26E consensus of ~$704M with growth slowing toward the +13% the Street expects, GAAP profit stays thin, and the stock settles between the low end of the Street's analyst target range and the median target.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Either Block terms are renegotiated with lower pricing, or Revenue Share step-ups widen the gap between volume and revenue enough to stall growth. We assume either route returns the quarterly operating margin to a loss, as in FY25's -7.4%, and takes the shares below the 52-week low of $14.80.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight Bear above Bull because of how each case is built. Bull needs two things at once: sustained revenue growth and continued cost discipline. Bear needs only one of two routes, a lower-priced Block arrangement or take-rate erosion. The routes are linked, since Block is one of the large customers whose volume drives Revenue Share step-ups, so we do not treat them as independent; the either/or structure alone justifies the heavier weight. The Base case carries the most weight because the six-month results support the consensus revenue path for FY26 without yet proving the earnings path for FY27. The probability-weighted value sits modestly above the current price, consistent with a HOLD rather than a BUY. We do not set Bear lower because of figures that do not depend on the share count: FY25 free cash flow of $160.8M, an FCF margin of 25.7% and no reported debt. That floor is weaker if the proxy share count is the right basis, which is one reason we stop at HOLD.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Marqeta reports a single reportable segment, so all FY25 revenue of $624.9M sits in one line and no product or geographic split is available. The economics turn on the platform services line, where pricing to customers and incentives from Card Networks both move with volume. TPV for FY25 was $382.5 billion per the 10-K risk factors.

moatFactors.name: Embedded infrastructure and switching costs
moatFactors.body: Per the 10-Q MD&A, customers embed Marqeta to avoid building complex compliance elements and customer support services themselves, and the company manages Issuing Bank relationships and Card Network rule compliance for them. That makes a working card program costly to move. The counter-case is that switching costs have not stopped large customers from winning price concessions, as the Risks section shows.

moatFactors.name: Volume-based network incentives
moatFactors.body: The 10-Q MD&A says Card Network incentives reach a higher cumulative rate as processing volumes increase, which rewards scale in costs of revenue. Part of that scale benefit is passed to customers through the Revenue Share step-up discussed under Growth, so the company keeps less of it than the incentive structure alone suggests.

moatFactors.name: Customer concentration
moatFactors.body: Pricing power with the customers that matter most is the weak point. The concentration set out under Risks means a moat built on embedded infrastructure still has to be renegotiated customer by customer.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat NARROW. The switching costs are real, because customers outsource compliance, bank sponsorship and network management rather than run them in-house. But the pricing evidence cuts the other way, given the concession to Block and the volume-linked pricing to customers covered elsewhere in this report. The 10-K risk factors also describe markets that are competitive and continuously evolving, without naming rivals. The advantage looks durable enough to retain customers, but not strong enough to hold price with the big accounts that carry concentration risk.

points: Volume growth is strong: the 10-Q MD&A reports Q2'26 TPV rising to $120,423 million from $91,386 million a year earlier, and the 10-K risk factors report FY25 TPV up 31%.

Revenue is growing more slowly than volume: Q2'26 revenue rose 17% while TPV grew considerably faster. The 10-Q MD&A says that, generally, as customers' processing volumes increase, the rates at which the company shares revenue with them increase, and that Revenue Share is recorded as a reduction to net revenue. We think that is one reason revenue lags TPV, though the filing does not say so or quantify it.

Consensus expects deceleration: FY26E revenue of ~$704M implies +13% growth after FY25 revenue of $624.9M grew +23.3%, with FY27E revenue of $807.2M. We see the FY26 estimate as reachable given the six-month results in the 10-Q.

The 10-K risk factors list expansion outside the United States, new offerings and a more diversified customer base among the drivers of future revenue growth. None is quantified in the facts, so we give them no weight in the Base case.

The counter-case is the slowdown already in the numbers: Q2'26 growth is below FY25's pace, and consensus expects a further step down for FY26. If the gap with TPV also widens, growth could fall below the Street's path.

management.leadership: The proxy statement dated April 21, 2026 lists Mike Milotich, Patti Kangwangkij, Todd Pollak and Crystal Sumner in its beneficial-ownership table under the heading for named executive officers, directors and director nominees, without giving their titles in the excerpt. The same proxy identifies Simon Khalaf as the former Chief Executive Officer and refers to a former Executive Chairman without naming the person in the excerpt. A change at the top is therefore evident, but the excerpt does not date Mr. Khalaf's separation, say why it happened or say who now leads the company. We cannot judge the current team on a record the sources do not provide; the operating expense discipline in the 2026 results is the clearest evidence available on execution.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation has leaned heavily toward buybacks. In the cash flow facts, share repurchases rose from $0.1B in FY22 to $0.4B in FY25, and FY25 repurchases were well above FY25 free cash flow. That gap, rather than any operating shortfall, is the main reason cash and equity fell even in a strong cash year. The company pays no dividend. The 10-K risk factors caution that the share repurchase program may not enhance long-term stockholder value and may reduce working capital. Our view is that buying back shares near the bottom of the 52-week range is defensible given the cash the business generates, but the FY25 pace drew down the buffer, and a pace closer to free cash flow would be the more prudent course while customer pricing remains uncertain.
management.governance: Per the proxy statement dated April 21, 2026, the Board determined that eight directors are independent under Nasdaq standards: Mmes. Atkinson, Cummings, Paul and Thomas and Messrs. Chokshi, Graf, Linville and Prasad. Jud Linville has served as independent Board Chair since June 2024, and the proxy cites his past role as Chief Executive Officer of Global Cards and Consumer Services at Citigroup Inc. The structure that matters most is the dual class. The 10-K risk factors state that it concentrates voting control with Class B holders, including directors, executive officers and their affiliates, and that it may depress the Class A trading price. For outside Class A holders, an independent chair and committee structure provide oversight, but their ability to shape contested decisions is limited, as the ownership figures below show.
management.insiderOwnership: As of April 15, 2026, per the proxy, Jason Gardner held 94.99% of Class B common stock and 46.92% of total voting power, and all directors and executive officers as a group held 48.62% of total voting power. The excerpt does not state Mr. Gardner's current role. Neither figure is a majority, so he cannot carry a vote alone. But he needs only a small share of the remaining votes to carry an ordinary resolution, and outside holders would have to vote almost as a bloc to defeat him. The proxy lists other 5% holders, including entities associated with T. Rowe Price Associates at 7.81% of voting power and entities associated with BlackRock, Inc. at 3.92%; the Vanguard row is listed without figures in the excerpt. For Class A investors, that means little practical leverage on contested matters.

idiosyncratic: Block concentration: the 10-K risk factors state that the company generates significant net revenue from a small number of customers, including Block, and that losing these relationships or renewing them on less favorable terms could hurt results. The August 2023 Block Amendment already allowed reduced pricing once, so this is a demonstrated risk rather than a hypothetical one. The pack gives no renewal date for Block; watch for any amendment disclosed in a future filing.

Take-rate compression: if volume growth concentrates in large customers, the Revenue Share step-up discussed under Growth could keep revenue growth lagging TPV. Watch the gap between TPV and revenue growth each quarter.
Valuation basis: the share-count question set out in the Valuation section means the market-cap multiples in this report carry more error than usual until a future filing resolves it.

Bank and network dependence: the 10-K risk factors state that the company relies on Issuing Banks and Card Networks, and the 10-Q MD&A says network incentives depend on hitting cumulative volume thresholds within an annual measurement period. We see a lost relationship as unlikely in the near term, but a missed incentive threshold would show up quickly as higher costs of revenue and a gross margin below the 69% of Q2'26. Watch gross margin and any disclosure of a change in Issuing Bank partners.
risks.systemic: The 10-Q MD&A states that management cannot predict how macroeconomic factors, including inflation, interest rates, geopolitical conflicts and uncertainty from potential tariffs, will affect processing volumes. Because revenue is tied to Interchange Fees and processing fees, a slowdown in consumer spending would flow through to revenue quickly. Regulation is a second channel: the 10-K risk factors note that rules applying directly and through Issuing Banks and Card Networks are subject to change and uncertain interpretation. Interest rates matter in a smaller way, because other income consists primarily of interest on short-term investments and cash deposits, and that income shrinks as cash is spent or as rates fall. We see these risks as cyclical rather than thesis-breaking, but they would amplify a Bear case driven by customer pricing.

body: HOLD, target range $15 to $21. Marqeta has shown it can grow revenue in the high teens, earn a GAAP profit through the six months ended June 30, 2026 and generate substantial free cash flow, and those qualities support the shares near the bottom of their 52-week range.

We stop short of BUY because volume growth is not fully reaching revenue, customer concentration remains unresolved, and the valuation basis is less certain than the headline multiples suggest. We would revisit the rating on a full GAAP-profitable year with revenue growth holding near the Q2'26 pace, or on disclosed Block terms that preserve pricing.
